text: Every secret, API key, and connection string an AI app needs has to come from somewhere — and the wrong answer, still disturbingly common, is pasted straight into the code.

The fix starts with a managed identity — a system-assigned identity enabled on the VM, App Service, or Function App itself, with a single checkbox at creation time. No secret gets issued to anyone, because there's no secret to leak.

That identity isn't just a checkbox, either — it's a real identity in Microsoft Entra ID, confirmed on the resource's own Identity blade where Status reads On, the same place it could be turned back off.

An identity on its own can't reach anything until it's granted access to something — in this course, usually a Key Vault holding the API keys and connection strings an AI app actually needs at runtime. That access is granted explicitly, through an access policy or RBAC role naming the identity — nothing is reachable by default just because an identity exists.

In code, the difference is one line: swap a ClientSecretCredential, which needs a client secret somewhere, for DefaultAzureCredential, which picks up the managed identity automatically — same SDK call, no client secret anywhere in the code, the config, or an environment variable.
No password in the code, because there's no password at all. Next up: the same deployment job, on a different cloud entirely.
